question_text: Find the locus of z in the Argand plane if Arg(z − 1) = π/2.

mark_split.label: Write z − 1 in terms of x and y and read the condition

But Arg(z − 1) = π/2 means z − 1 lies on the POSITIVE imaginary axis, so y > 0 as well; on the lower half of the line x = 1 the argument is −π/2, and at z = 1 it is undefined. The card writes the locus as x = 1 with y > 0 (the half-line above the point (1, 0)) and records the book's printed line in the last step's 'why'. recall_prompt: Say how you would find the locus — what z − 1 is in x and y, and what an argument of π/2 forces on its two parts.
insider_note: The answer is a half-line, not the whole line x = 1: an argument of π/2 forces the real part of z − 1 to be 0 and its imaginary part to be positive, so y > 0 must appear next to x = 1. Without y > 0 the line includes points whose argument is −π/2.

steps.margin_note: First mark. z − 1 = (x − 1) + iy. An argument of π/2 means the number points straight up the imaginary axis: real part 0, imaginary part positive.

steps.why: A number with argument π/2 is a positive multiple of i. That is two conditions at once — real part zero AND imaginary part positive — and both are needed to describe the locus exactly.
common_mistakes: Writing z − 1 = x − 1 + y, dropping the i.
Reading Arg = π/2 as 'the number is purely imaginary' and forgetting that the imaginary part must also be positive.

steps.label: State the locus
steps.margin_note: Second mark. x − 1 = 0 and y > 0: the vertical half-line above the point (1, 0).

lines.text: ∴ Locus of z: x = 1, with y > 0

recall.must_convey: That the locus is x = 1 with y > 0 — the half of the vertical line x = 1 that lies above the real axis.
accept: x minus one is zero and y is positive, so the locus is the line x equals one above the real axis
the locus is x equals one with y greater than zero

steps.why: On the line x = 1, points above the real axis have Arg(z − 1) = π/2 and points below have −π/2, while z = 1 itself has no argument. So the locus is the upper half-line only. The book prints the answer as the whole line x − 1 = 0; the y > 0 condition is what makes the answer exact, and a teacher marking to the book's key will accept x − 1 = 0 as the main line.
common_mistakes: Giving the whole line x = 1, which includes points with argument −π/2.
Giving y = 0 instead of x = 1 — that would be argument 0 or π.
